description: ASEAN-specific pathway exploring impact of unconditional NDCs and existing policies.
pathwayDescription:
The ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) acts as the ASEAN energy data center and knowledge hub and produces the ACE ASEAN Energy Outlook providing energy pathways for Southeast Asia. The ACE ASEAN Member States Targets Scenario (ATS) is an exploratory pathway which assumes that every ASEAN member state fully achieves its unconditional transition targets on time, including unconditional goals set via Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). This pathway models the impact of existing policies, such as national power development plans (PDPs), and the implementation of these stated targets. The ATS pathway models more ambitious energy efficiency targets, as well as a faster deployment of low-carbon energy technologies, especially from renewable energy. The ATS pathway does not include more aspirational national objectives, such as conditional NDCs or long-term net zero goals. For examples of pathways that include these policies, see the ACE Regional Aspiration Scenario (RAS) and IEA Announced Pledges Scenario (APS).

Power generation emissions decline -2.4% per year, resulting in a total decrease of 74% relative to power emissions in the Baseline Scenario. However, the ATS pathway projects to an average annual emissions increase of 0.8% across the full energy sector.

coreDrivers.policies: National renewable-energy and efficiency targets, power development plans, energy-access measures and unconditional NDCs drive the outcomes of the ATS pathway.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Average annual Power investment rises from USD 34.8bn in 2023–2030 to USD 46.3bn in 2041–2050. This comes from significant investment in solar and wind that more than offsets the lower fossil fuel investment needs compared to BAS.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP growth are a common underlying demand driver across all ACE scenarios and extracted from World Bank and ADB projections.

dependencies.dependency_description: National PDPs, renewable energy and energy efficiency targets, and unconditional NDCs directly determine the ATS power build-out.
Implementing diverse national plans and standards is necessary, but the report does not quantify permitting or market-rule constraints.
Introdction of nuclear power generation to the region may may require education for public acceptance.
Stable electrification rates limit on adoption of new end-use technologies.
A 69.4% renewable capacity share by 2050 (more than double the share in the start year) increases grid-integration needs, although ATS does not model energy storage.

Faster uptake of RE means that net import of natural gas starts in 2030, later than in the BAS pathway. Land use for biofuels in ATS is similar to that of BAS. The increase land use for RE therefore raises overall land use requirements. Pathway targets are not constrained by RE potential.
Faster fossil retirement in ATS creates materially larger job losses and retraining needs than BAS. The net difference in energy jobs is not very large though.
